explain.say: In 1829 James Simpson ran London river water slowly through a bed of sand for the Chelsea waterworks, and it came out sparkling. Today's rapid gravity filters do the same job about forty times faster. On the board is a cut through one: water on top, then coal, sand and gravel, with drains at the bottom.

explain.say: Here is a water works in 3D. The sand filter and the chlorination stage near the end are the last two barriers before the clear water tank. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: Rapid sand filters and breakpoint chlorination: the last two barriers

explain.say: Look at the fine sand. It is not a sieve: the gaps between grains are bigger than most flocs. Instead flocs stick to grains all the way down, so the whole bed works. Water runs down at about five metres per hour. For our six hundred and twenty five cubic metres an hour, that is a hundred and twenty five square metres of filter, say four filters of about thirty one each.

explain.say: As dirt builds up, the water struggles to get through. Every day or two the filter is backwashed: air and clean water are blown up through the underdrains, lifting the sand so the dirt floats off. Slow sand filters skip this; they run at about a tenth of a metre per hour and a living slime layer on top eats germs. Why would a busy city prefer the rapid kind?

draw.text: Slow sand: about 0.1 to 0.2 m/h. Rapid gravity: about 5 to 10 m/h.

explain.say: Less land! Now the final barrier, chlorine. Watch the curve as the dose rises. First, iron and other chemicals use some up. Then chlorine joins with ammonia to make weaker chloramines, and the residual climbs. More chlorine destroys them, so the residual falls to a dip, the breakpoint. Past it, every extra milligram stays as strong free chlorine.

Killing germs needs strength and time together, the CT value: half a milligram per litre held for thirty minutes gives fifteen. That is why water works have contact tanks before the pipes. Superb! Challenge: past the breakpoint, if you add one more milligram per litre, how much does the residual rise?

draw.text: CT = C × t = 0.5 mg/L × 30 min = 15 mg·min/L

faq.q: What is a rapid gravity sand filter?
faq.a: A concrete box holding layers of anthracite, sand and gravel over underdrains. Water flows down by gravity at about 5 to 10 metres per hour, and the bed is cleaned by backwashing.
asks: How does a rapid sand filter work?

faq.q: How does sand filtration remove particles?
faq.a: Mostly by depth filtration: particles smaller than the gaps stick to sand grains through the whole bed, rather than being sieved at the surface.
asks: Why use sand in a filter?

faq.a: Backwashing reverses the flow, blowing air and clean water up through the bed to lift the sand and flush out trapped dirt, usually every one to three days.
asks: How is a sand filter cleaned?

faq.a: It is adding enough chlorine to destroy the chloramines formed with ammonia. The residual dips to a minimum, the breakpoint, and any chlorine added after it remains as free chlorine, the strong disinfectant.
CT is the disinfectant concentration times the contact time. Half a milligram per litre held for 30 minutes gives a CT of 15 milligram minutes per litre; each germ needs a certain CT.

facts: Slow sand filters run at roughly 0.1 to 0.2 m/h, while rapid gravity filters run at roughly 5 to 10 m/h.
Past the breakpoint, the free chlorine residual rises about one-for-one with each extra mg/L of dose.

quiz.say: Chlorine added beyond the breakpoint mostly stays as…
quiz.show: Chlorine added beyond the breakpoint mostly stays as…
quiz.why: After the breakpoint the chloramines are destroyed, so extra chlorine remains as free chlorine.

wrong.1: Chloramines form before the breakpoint and are destroyed by it.
wrong.2: Alum is the coagulant, not a form of chlorine.
